message:
3 ways to protect yourself from LSASS dump removal

⏺ Why it matters : Dumping LSASS is a super classic technique for stealing credentials from memory. Hackers use ProcDump, comsvcs.dll, MiniDumpWriteDump, and even PowerShell scripts to extract secrets.

⏺ Why simply disabling ProcDump won't help : remove ProcDump - the hacker will launch rundll32 comsvcs.dll, MiniDump. Disable PowerShell - he will just bring his utility. You need to act differently.

3 levels of protection that really work:

1️⃣ RunAsPPL — put up a shield from handles: Windows can run LSASS in protected mode (Protected Process Light). In this mode, even SYSTEM processes cannot simply open LSASS with the necessary rights. How to enable:

[HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa]
"RunAsPPL"=dword:00000001

Yes, this way you can break the curved EDR, but the protection is not always without side effects...

2️⃣ Sysmon catches extra hands: Sysmon config that will catch any attempt to access LSASS:

<ProcessAccess onmatch="include">
<TargetImage condition="contains">lsass.exe</TargetImage>
</ProcessAccess>

And now any attempt to “peep” at LSASS is in the logs. All that remains is to teach SIEM to react.

3️⃣ EDR: looking towards CreateFile and OpenProcess: Setting up alerts for processes that open lsass.exe with PROCESS_VM_READ, PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION rights. Especially if it is powershell.exe, rundll32.exe or some notepad.exe from AppData.

Cyber security is a big field but lets assume you are looking at the pentest part of it, it is a good move. The best way to understand this is to understand how attackers think and how defenders respond. For now, don't put the emphasis on tools or platforms, but focus on capturing how systems, networks, and logs work. Learn to read Windows and Linux logs, understand how authentication flows occur, what normal traffic looks like, and what stands out. When you start to see patterns, it will click.

From there, start reading reports on real-world attacks (Mandiant, CISA, etc.). Try to mentally walk through the kill chain. Don't jump into exploits yet: first understand what an attacker is trying to do, not just how. Once you acquire this mindset, the transition to attack will come naturally.

You are already on the right track. Keep digging, stay curious, and don't rush. The deeper your foundation, the more skilled you will be, whether you are defending or breaking.

And this is just an introduction.
The rest is up to you ,good luck! :)

message:
Are you new to the realm of hacking?🐰

Anything includes: Abbreviations, Phrases, Words, and Techniques.*The list is in alphabetical order for convenience!*

Abbreviations

? DDoS = Distributed Denial of Service

? DrDoS = Distributed Reflected Denial of Service Attack, uses a list of reflection servers or other methods such as DNS to spoof an attack to look like it's coming from multiple ips. Amplification of power in the attack COULD occur.

? FTP =File Transfer Protocol. Used for transferring files over an FTP server.

? FUD = Fully Undetectable

? Hex =In computer science, hexadecimal refers to base-16 numbers. These are numbers that use digits in the range: 0123456789ABCDEF. In the C programming language (as well as Java, JavaScript, C++, and other places), hexadecimal numbers are prefixed by a 0x. In this manner, one can tell that the number 0x80 is equivalent to 128 decimal, not 80 decimal.

? HTTP =Hyper Text Transfer Protocol. The foundation of data communication for the World Wide Web.

? IRC = Internet Relay Chat. Transmiting text messages in real time between online users.

? JDB =Java drive-by, a very commonly used web-based exploit which allows an attacker to download and execute malicious code locally on a slave's machine through a widely known java vulnerability.

? Malware =Malicious Software

? Nix = Unix based operating system, usually refered to here when refering to DoS'ing.

? POP3 =This is the most popular protocol for picking up e-mail from a server.

? R.A.T = Remote Administration Tool

? SDB = Silent drive-by, using a zero day web-based exploit to hiddenly and un-detectably download and execute malicious code on a slave's system. (similar to a JDB however no notification or warning is given to the user)

? SE = Social Engineering

? Skid =Script Kid/Script Kiddie

? SMTP =A TCP/IP protocol used in sending and receiving e-mail.

? SQL =Structured Query Language. It's a programming language, that used to communicate with databases and DBMS. Can go along with a word after it, such as "SQL Injection."

? SSH =Secure Shell, used to connect to Virtual Private Servers.

? TCP = Transmission Control Protocol, creates connections and exchanges packets of data.

? UDP =User Datagram Protocol, An alternative data transport to TCP used for DNS, Voice over IP, and file sharing.

? VPN =Virtual Private Network

? VPS =Virtual Private Server

? XSS (CSS) = Cross Site Scripting

Words

? Algorithm = A series of steps specifying which actions to take in which order.

? ANSI Bomb = ANSI.SYS key-remapping commands consist of cryptic-looking text that specifies, using ansi numeric codes to redefine keys.

? Back Door = Something a hacker leaves behind on a system in order to be able to get back in at a later time.

? Binary = A numbering system in which there are only two possible values for each digit: 0 and 1.

? Black Hat = A hacker who performs illegal actions to do with hacking online. (Bad guy, per se)

? Blue Hat =A blue hat hacker is someone outside computer security consulting firms who is used to bug test a system prior to its launch, looking for exploits so they can be closed. Microsoft also uses the term BlueHat to represent a series of security briefing events.

? Bot = A piece of malware that connects computer to an attacker commonly using the HTTP or IRC protocal to await malicous instructions

? Botnet = Computers infected by worms or Trojans and taken over by hackers and brought into networks to send spam, more viruses, or launch denial of service attacks.

? Buffer Overflow = A classic exploit that sends more data than a programmer expects to receive. Buffer overflows are one of the most common programming errors, and the ones most likely to slip through quality assurance testing.

✦•━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━•✦

message:
💠 Cyber Security Roadmap 💠

**1. Computer Operating System Basics**

**A. Foundations**
- Objective: Understand the fundamentals of computer operating systems.

**B. Topics to Cover**
- Basic Concepts:
  - Types of operating systems (Windows, Linux, macOS, etc.)
  - Processes, threads, and multitasking
  - Memory management and virtual memory
  - File systems and storage management

**2. Networking Fundamentals**

**A. Foundations**
- Objective: Grasp essential networking concepts and protocols.

**B. Topics to Cover**
- Basic Networking Concepts:
  - OSI Model and TCP/IP stack
  - IP addressing (IPv4 and IPv6)
  - Subnetting and CIDR notation
  - DNS, DHCP, and ARP
  - Routing and switching basics
  - Network security fundamentals

**3. Windows Operating System**

**A. Foundations**
- Objective: Familiarize yourself with Windows OS architecture and management.

**B. Topics to Cover**
- Windows Basics:
  - File systems (NTFS, FAT)
  - User accounts and permissions
  - Task scheduling and services
  - Registry and Group Policy
  - Event logs and auditing

**C. Windows Exploitation**
- Objective: Learn about vulnerabilities and exploitation techniques in Windows systems.

**D. Topics to Cover**
- Common Vulnerabilities:
  - Exploitation methods (e.g., buffer overflow, DLL hijacking)
  - Privilege escalation techniques
  - Tools like Metasploit for exploitation

**4. Android Operating System**

A. Foundations
- Objective: Understand the Android OS architecture and security model.

**B. Topics to Cover**
- Android Basics:
  - Android file system structure
  - Application components (Activities, Services, Broadcast Receivers, Content Providers)
  - Permissions and security settings

**C. Android Exploitation**
- Objective: Explore vulnerabilities and exploitation techniques specific to Android.

**D. Topics to Cover**
- Common Vulnerabilities:
  - Reverse engineering APK files
  - Exploiting insecure app components (e.g., insecure storage, intent spoofing)
  - Rooting and jailbreaking techniques

**5. Linux Operating System**

**A. Foundations**
- Objective: Gain proficiency in using and administering Linux systems.

**B. Topics to Cover**
- Linux Basics:
  - Command-line usage and basic commands
  - File system hierarchy (directories and permissions)
  - Process management and multitasking
  - Shell scripting (Bash scripting)

**C. Linux Exploitation**
- Objective: Learn about vulnerabilities and exploitation techniques in Linux systems.

**D. Topics to Cover**
- Common Vulnerabilities:
  - Privilege escalation (e.g., sudo misconfigurations)
  - Exploiting services and daemons (e.g., SSH, Apache)
  - Post-exploitation activities (pivoting, lateral movement)

**6. Web Exploitation and Ethical Hacking**

**A. Foundations**
- Objective: Understand how web applications work and common security issues.

**B. Topics to Cover**
- Web Fundamentals:
  - HTTP/HTTPS protocols
  - Web application architecture (client-server model)
  - Basics of HTML, JavaScript, PHP, SQL

**C. Ethical Hacking Techniques**
- Objective: Learn ethical hacking methodologies and tools for web applications.

**D. Topics to Cover**
- Common Attacks and Techniques:
  - Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), SQL Injection, CSRF
  - Web application scanning and enumeration
  - Tools like Burp Suite for web application testing

**Learning Paths for Beginners**

1. Beginner Level :
   - Start with foundational courses or books on computer operating systems and networking.
   - Practice basic commands and concepts on both Windows and Linux systems.
   - Understand the fundamentals of Android security and app development.

**2. Intermediate Level :**
   - Dive deeper into Windows and Linux exploitation techniques.
   - Explore Android vulnerabilities and rooting techniques.
   - Begin studying web exploitation techniques and ethical hacking methodologies.

**3. Advanced Level :**
   - Choose a specialization based on your interests (e.g., Windows/Linux exploitation, Android security, web application security).
   - Aim for certifications like OSCP (Offensive Security Certified Professional) or relevant GIAC certifications depending on your chosen path.

**What is an OTP?
**“One-Time Password” (OTP) refers to a security mechanism that uses an authenticator app to verify users by providing them with a unique, single-use code for account access. This code expires after one use and cannot be used again. Typically, these passwords are delivered via SMS, email, or through authenticator apps on smartphones and other devices. OTPs are designed to enhance account security by removing the risk of a password being compromised due to leaks or password reuse.

How to start hacking...the step by step guide with some tips...from my experience
 
🔱What you need to learn—— 
1. Computer Basics  (how the hell anything works..like what happens when you press a key ...from software level to hardware level).
2. Networking  (to understand how things works {very crucial})
3. Get familiar with command line  (windows+linux, these are what you will be dealing with in real life scenarios)
4. Programming languages  ( start with python and bash, as they can help you in creating or modifying many tools, the rest depends on your domain, like if you want to go on websites testing then you should learn html, javascript, sql, a little bit php and etc. and if you want to go to android pentesting then you have to know about C, java and other related languages, you can research about them through chatGPT or grok)
5. Start playing CTFs and solve labs from tryhackme and hackthebox (to practice and more practice)

⭕️Use tryhackme.com for learning concepts and practicing at the same time, when you are confident, use vulnhub.com then head over to hackthebox and other good platforms like hacktricks which will tell you more about other techniques 
⭕️tryhackme will tell you about some hacking tools, basic stuff, use google/chatGPT/grokAI/otherAIs about them to learn more, and what else we can do with those tools and services
⭕️Specialization can be proven with certifications, though they are only for creating impression and you should only go after them only if you can afford them, otherwise there are alot of achievements which you can add in your resume and CV, like the vulnerabilities you have founded(can include swag and hall of fame you got from bug bounty/VDPs), your projects, number of labs you have solved, these all free things really tells the interviewer about how much practically skilled you are

⭕️CERTIFICATES example: CCNA, CEH(though many companies don't recognise it now since it can be purchased), OSCP, OSWP, etc. (use google/chatGPT/grokAI to know more about  other certificates, there are HUNDREDS) can create quite good impression if you can afford them

🔱FOR SOURCES: 
1️⃣ Free youtube videos
     
      MUST TO MENTION YOUTUBE CHANNELS
          ◆ Vyuha.Infinity
          1. Network chuck
          2. Bitten Tech
          3. IppSec 
          4. Hackersploit
          5. NullByte
          6. John Hammond
          7. TheCyberMentor
          8. TechRaj
          9. Tech 69 (Don't judge by his SUBS)
          10. HACKADAY
          11. LiveOverflow
          12. TechChip
          13. thenewboston
          14. Hacking Simplified
          15. Loi Liang  Yang
         
2️⃣ There is alot of free resources available on the internet, like youtube, reddit, alison, mygreatlearning, simplilearn, telegram, etc. you have to RESEARCH about them, take knowledge from whichever sources you can find, but it doesn't mean that you have to blindly take any course, read it's reviews first
3️⃣ BOOOOOKSSSSS, google any topic and type "books for topic", whatever you get start reading, if you have no previous knowledge. if you have some, you will be able to identify the right book yourself 

🌀IMPORTANT THING:
Blogs and forums are very useful to learn "ADVANCED STUFF" so try to find some less known/hidden from forums too

NOTE:

Don't skip the theory part and do not use tools only, learn what and how are they doing some stuff, cause for really exploiting a system you need to learn what is happening in the background. else you will only be a script kiddie 

You can exploit some old system by using already made tools without knowing what the hell is going on in the background, but this will be useless if you want to exploit a new system, to create your own tools you must have knowledge about everything

⚜️ONE RULE MUST NOT FORGET
(About books v/s videos):
"videos" are easy to learn from, they tell about the application part, BUT books, blogs and articles(if they are good) will teach you theory and application
and here in this field, theory along with practical skills is also highly crucial for "REAL HACKING"

✈️ Hacking Airplanes – Is it Really Possible?

Hey buddy, how are you doing?

You won’t believe it… I swear I was just thinking about you today!

But seriously, have you ever heard about hacking an airplane?

“Come on, Spider… hacking a plane? You sound crazy!”

Well my friend, no… it’s not crazy at all 👀


---

🎯 The Topic: Hacking Airplanes ✈️

Back in 2014–2015,
a security researcher named Chris Roberts managed to hack a real airplane… while he was actually on board!

How?

He discovered a vulnerability in the plane’s IFE (In-Flight Entertainment) system.
He created a malicious USB that contained an exploit script targeting the system.
Once he plugged it into the USB port of the aircraft… boom 💥
He was inside the plane’s systems!


---

🛰️ Other Attack Methods?

Definitely, bro.

🔁 GPS Spoofing

This is when you send fake GPS signals to the airplane.
You trick it into thinking it’s in a different location — making it land somewhere it shouldn't.

A website called OPSGROUP even confirmed multiple incidents like that — especially in places like:

Cairo

Baghdad

Palestine (yes, that place you know they never mention)


This made some airplanes go back to old-school, manual navigation systems.


---

📂 So… Is Data Ever Leaked?

Absolutely.

In 2014, a major company called SITA — which serves over 90% of global airlines —
was hacked. Tons of passenger data was leaked!

Why?
Most of these systems run on Linux.

Let me give you a simple example:

You’re sitting on a plane, right? You got the little screen in front of you.
Try typing the word:

Spider spider spider spider
Spider spider spider spider
Spider spider spider spider

If the system crashes or exits the program — that’s a sign of a bug or vulnerability in the plane’s software 😬


---

🧠 Any Other Ways to Hack a Plane?

Well, as of writing this article — and to my current knowledge —
there aren’t many more realistic ways to hack a plane from the inside, other than what I mentioned.


---

🎭 What About Social Engineering?

That’s a great point.

Can it work? Yes.
Can it also fail miserably? Yes 😅

✅ It might work if someone is pretending to be a high-ranking official, or engineer, or anyone with access — and sneaks in a malicious USB device.

❌ But in real life?
You really gonna walk up to a flight attendant and say:

> "Excuse me, can you plug in this USB for me?" 🤦🏻‍♂️




---

🔐 So, How Do Airlines Protect Themselves Now?

Simple really.

1. Old-school policies:

Some airlines now physically disconnect Wi-Fi or USB access from critical systems.



2. Custom Security Systems:

They build firewalls and protection layers specifically designed for aviation networks.



3. Network Segmentation:

Entertainment systems are separated from flight controls, reducing risk.





---

✅ Final Thoughts

Yes, hacking planes is technically possible — but extremely difficult.

Cybersecurity awareness in aviation is growing rapidly.

Companies are learning from past incidents and building more secure systems every day.



---

Thank you so much for reading the article.
I really hope I was able to teach you at least one cool thing today ✨

And don’t go too far…
Something big is coming soon 🤍

message:
💠 Cyber Security Roadmap 💠

1. Computer Operating System Basics

A. Foundations
- Objective: Understand the fundamentals of computer operating systems.

B. Topics to Cover
- Basic Concepts:
  - Types of operating systems (Windows, Linux, macOS, etc.)
  - Processes, threads, and multitasking
  - Memory management and virtual memory
  - File systems and storage management

2. Networking Fundamentals

A. Foundations
- Objective: Grasp essential networking concepts and protocols.

B. Topics to Cover
- Basic Networking Concepts:
  - OSI Model and TCP/IP stack
  - IP addressing (IPv4 and IPv6)
  - Subnetting and CIDR notation
  - DNS, DHCP, and ARP
  - Routing and switching basics
  - Network security fundamentals

3. Windows Operating System

A. Foundations
- Objective: Familiarize yourself with Windows OS architecture and management.

B. Topics to Cover
- Windows Basics:
  - File systems (NTFS, FAT)
  - User accounts and permissions
  - Task scheduling and services
  - Registry and Group Policy
  - Event logs and auditing

C. Windows Exploitation
- Objective: Learn about vulnerabilities and exploitation techniques in Windows systems.

D. Topics to Cover
- Common Vulnerabilities:
  - Exploitation methods (e.g., buffer overflow, DLL hijacking)
  - Privilege escalation techniques
  - Tools like Metasploit for exploitation

4. Android Operating System

A. Foundations
- Objective: Understand the Android OS architecture and security model.

B. Topics to Cover
- Android Basics:
  - Android file system structure
  - Application components (Activities, Services, Broadcast Receivers, Content Providers)
  - Permissions and security settings

C. Android Exploitation
- Objective: Explore vulnerabilities and exploitation techniques specific to Android.

D. Topics to Cover
- Common Vulnerabilities:
  - Reverse engineering APK files
  - Exploiting insecure app components (e.g., insecure storage, intent spoofing)
  - Rooting and jailbreaking techniques

5. Linux Operating System

A. Foundations
- Objective: Gain proficiency in using and administering Linux systems.

B. Topics to Cover
- Linux Basics:
  - Command-line usage and basic commands
  - File system hierarchy (directories and permissions)
  - Process management and multitasking
  - Shell scripting (Bash scripting)

C. Linux Exploitation
- Objective: Learn about vulnerabilities and exploitation techniques in Linux systems.

D. Topics to Cover
- Common Vulnerabilities:
  - Privilege escalation (e.g., sudo misconfigurations)
  - Exploiting services and daemons (e.g., SSH, Apache)
  - Post-exploitation activities (pivoting, lateral movement)

6. Web Exploitation and Ethical Hacking

A. Foundations
- Objective: Understand how web applications work and common security issues.

B. Topics to Cover
- Web Fundamentals:
  - HTTP/HTTPS protocols
  - Web application architecture (client-server model)
  - Basics of HTML, JavaScript, PHP, SQL

C. Ethical Hacking Techniques
- Objective: Learn ethical hacking methodologies and tools for web applications.

D. Topics to Cover
- Common Attacks and Techniques:
  - Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), SQL Injection, CSRF
  - Web application scanning and enumeration
  - Tools like Burp Suite for web application testing

Learning Paths for Beginners

1. Beginner Level :
   - Start with foundational courses or books on computer operating systems and networking.
   - Practice basic commands and concepts on both Windows and Linux systems.
   - Understand the fundamentals of Android security and app development.

2. Intermediate Level :
   - Dive deeper into Windows and Linux exploitation techniques.
   - Explore Android vulnerabilities and rooting techniques.
   - Begin studying web exploitation techniques and ethical hacking methodologies.

3. Advanced Level :
   - Choose a specialization based on your interests (e.g., Windows/Linux exploitation, Android security, web application security).
   - Aim for certifications like OSCP (Offensive Security Certified Professional) or relevant GIAC certifications depending on your chosen path.

message:
Understanding Brute-Force Attacks
​A brute-force attack is a trial-and-error method used to guess login credentials, encryption keys, or hidden web pages. It involves systematically checking every possible combination until the correct one is found.
​How it Works: The attacker uses a tool to automate the process of submitting numerous guesses against a login form or authentication service.
​Dictionary Attack: Tries passwords from a pre-compiled list of common or compromised passwords (a wordlist).
​Simple Brute-Force: Tries every possible combination of characters (numbers, letters, symbols) up to a certain length.
​Ethical and Legal Security Testing
​Tools like Hydra and Medusa are legitimate parts of a security professional's toolkit when used for:
​Penetration Testing (Pen-testing): Testing the security of your own networks and applications to find weaknesses before malicious actors do.
​Security Auditing: Verifying that authentication mechanisms are robust and cannot be easily cracked by automated tools.
​It is illegal and unethical to use these tools against any system or account you do not own or have explicit, written permission to test. Unauthorized access is a crime in nearly all jurisdictions.
​Defensive Measures Against Brute-Force Attacks
​The focus for anyone managing a website or account should be on implementing strong defenses against these attacks

message:
Defensive Strategy Description
Rate Limiting Restricting the number of login attempts from a single IP address or user account within a short timeframe.
Account Lockout Temporarily or permanently locking an account after a small number of failed login attempts (e.g., 5).
Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) Requiring a secondary verification code (usually from a phone app or SMS) in addition to a password. This renders a brute-forced password useless without the second factor.
CAPTCHA Requiring the user to solve a simple challenge (like identifying images or typing distorted text) that is difficult for automated bots.
Strong Passwords Encouraging users to use long, complex, and unique passwords that are extremely difficult to guess.
IP Blacklisting Blocking IP addresses that show suspicious patterns of repeated failed logins.

message:
Focus on Ethical Hacking and Defense 🛡️
If your interest is in cybersecurity and penetration testing, I strongly encourage you to pursue ethical hacking (often called "white-hat" hacking). This field is about using the same skills and tools to identify and fix security vulnerabilities, but only on systems you own or have explicit, legal permission to test.
Tools like Hydra and Medusa are used legally by security professionals for tasks like:
Testing the strength of a new server's default configuration (e.g., SSH or FTP access).
Auditing a custom web application's login form within a controlled, authorized environment.
Defensive Countermeasures
The best way to understand these attacks is to learn how to defend against them. If you are responsible for a website or account, the critical steps to protect against brute-force attacks are:
Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): This is the single most effective defense. Even if an attacker guesses the password, they won't have the second factor (e.g., a code from a phone app).
Rate Limiting and Account Lockout: Restrict the number of failed login attempts from a single IP address over a short period. For example, lock the account after 5 failed tries.
CAPTCHA: Implement challenges that bots cannot easily solve to prevent automated login attempts.
Strong Password Policies: Enforce long, complex, and unique passwords that are nearly impossible to guess in a brute-force scenario.
Resources for Ethical Learning
If you want to learn penetration testing legally, you should use controlled environments designed for education, such as:
Virtual Labs: Platforms like TryHackMe and Hack The Box offer "Capture The Flag" (CTF) challenges and virtual labs where you can practice penetration testing techniques legally and safely.
Security Courses: Courses that lead to certifications like Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) or CompTIA PenTest+ teach these concepts with a focus on defense, legality, and ethics.
Vulnerable Systems: Practice on intentionally vulnerable virtual machines, such as Metasploitable or those from OWASP's Broken Web Applications Project, to understand how attacks work without harming any live targets.
